output.brief: The evidence points to the revised merit scholarship schedule, not the Admissions Office, as the main reason for the enrolment drop. Applications, admits and GPA all rose, so the applicant pool was not the problem. Yield fell sharply only in the tiers where awards were cut: Dean's went from $14,000 to $9,000 and Merit from $9,000 to $5,000. Yield was flat for Presidential awards, which were unchanged, and for students with no merit award. Early-action students got decisions on time yet their yield fell almost as much as regular-decision students' (7.4 vs 7.5 points). That argues against slow decisions as the main driver. The regular-decision delays were real, and the cause of them is unresolved. Reader cuts and the unstable portal module overlapped, and nobody has measured which mattered more. The missing-transcript complaints are unverified. I am fairly confident, though the data is not split by round within each tier. Next steps: do not replace the director on this evidence. Take the scholarship schedule back to the finance committee with a modelled proposal to restore awards in the tiers where yield fell, before award letters go out. Also set a turnaround target for regular decisions, and audit the transcript problem before ordering any vendor rebuild.
output.methodChoice: Collected X1 (yield by round) and X13 (yield by scholarship tier) to separate the turnaround and scholarship explanations.
